title: Write a query to find duplicate customer emails (`GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`), and explain why the application-level `if (!emailExists) insert` check is NOT enough under concurrency and must be backed by a DB `UNIQUE` constraint (the app validates, the database enforces).
shortTitle: Duplicate Customer Emails and Why App-Level Checks Need a DB UNIQUE Constraint

s1_definition.oneliner: `GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` finds dupes, but the app's check-then-insert races under concurrency: only a DB `UNIQUE` constraint truly prevents duplicates.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Detection query** – `SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)), COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` finds existing duplicates with normalization.
- **Check-then-insert race** – the app's `if (!emailExists) insert` is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race; two threads can both see "not exists" and both insert.
- **UNIQUE constraint** – the database enforces uniqueness atomically at write time; the second concurrent insert fails with a unique-violation error.
- **App validates, DB enforces** – the application check gives a friendly message in the common case; the constraint guarantees correctness under concurrency.
- **Case-insensitive uniqueness** – use a functional unique index on `LOWER(email)` or PostgreSQL's `citext` type.
s1_definition.analogy: Two people walk up to two different counters at National Bank of India at the same second, both wanting to register rajesh@x.com. Each teller checks "is this email taken?" and both see "no" because neither registration is saved yet. Both say "go ahead." The email now exists twice. The only fix is a rule stamped on the ledger itself that physically refuses a second identical email.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Thread A                              Thread B
  ────────                              ────────
  SELECT (email exists?) ──▶ No         SELECT (email exists?) ──▶ No
       │                                     │
       ▼                                     ▼
  INSERT rajesh@nbi.com ──▶ ✓           INSERT rajesh@nbi.com
       │                                     │
       │                                     ▼
       │                          ┌──────────────────────┐
       │                          │ UNIQUE constraint:   │
       │                          │ REJECT (23505 error) │
       │                          └──────────────────────┘
       ▼
  COMMIT ✓

  Without constraint: both succeed ──▶ DUPLICATE!
  With constraint: second fails  ──▶ SAFE
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To find duplicate emails, group by a normalized email and keep groups with a count above one. But the more important point is why they exist. An application check like `if (!emailExists) insert` is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race: under concurrency two requests both see "not present" and both insert, producing a duplicate.

The only robust fix is a database UNIQUE constraint, because the database is the single serialization point that every concurrent client funnels through, and it enforces uniqueness atomically at write time. The application check remains useful for a fast, friendly response in the common non-racing case, but it is an optimization, not the guarantee.

At the National Bank of India a customer double-clicked submit on a slow connection, two requests both passed the check-then-insert, and two accounts ended up sharing one email, which later broke password reset. Rajesh cleaned up the existing duplicates and added a case-insensitive unique index so it can never recur.

The principle generalizes: any invariant that must never be violated, such as unique account numbers, one active loan per customer, or a non-negative balance, belongs as a database constraint. The application validates, the database enforces.

Remember one sentence: the app's check-then-insert races, so back every uniqueness rule with a DB UNIQUE constraint.

---

keyPoints: GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 with LOWER and TRIM normalization finds existing duplicates.
The check-then-insert pattern is a TOCTOU race: two threads can both see "not exists" and both insert.
A UNIQUE constraint enforces uniqueness atomically at write time, catching the concurrent race.
For case-insensitive uniqueness, use a functional unique index on LOWER(email) or citext.
The app validates for a friendly message; the database enforces for correctness under concurrency.
INSERT ON CONFLICT (upsert) avoids the check entirely for an optimistic approach.
Any invariant that must never be violated belongs as a database constraint, not just application logic.
